entry.title: [PATCH v2 0/3] IPE: add a dedicated policy keyring

div.pre:
Add a dedicated ".ipe" keyring for IPE policy-signature verification, allowing userspace to provision IPE-specific policy-signing certificates. Systems that do not provision the keyring retain their existing behavior.
This series is based on commit 48f936e302a9 ("ipe: update the project and test suite links") from ipe/next. The BPF, dm-verity, and fs-verity well-known key IDs are now in mainline [1]; KEY_SPEC_IPE_KEYRING follows these IDs at -12. The series should be rebased once that work is available in ipe/next.
IPE currently checks the keyring's entry count directly. A separate keys RFC proposes keyring_is_empty() to encapsulate this check [2]. This series does not depend on that RFC; it should use the helper if available in the submission base.
Testing: - Built x86_64 kernels with GCC 15.2.0 and Clang/LLD 21.1.8. - Passed all 33 in-tree IPE parser KUnit cases under QEMU/KVM. - Passed all 2,364 IPE CI cases under QEMU/KVM, including eight new .ipe keyring cases [3]. The CI changes are in draft PR [4].
[1] https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=62c457528529 [2] https://lore.kernel.org/r/user4@example.test [3] The CI run used a local compatibility adjustment to locate usr/gen_init_cpio on this kernel base. [4] https://github.com/Integrity-Policy-Enforcement/ci/pull/4
Signed-off-by: Manuel Huber <user5@example.test> --- Changes in v2: - Drop the RFC designation. - Replace ipe.keyring_unsealed with default-off CONFIG_SECURITY_IPE_KEYRING; leave provisioning and restriction of the enabled keyring to userspace. - Require restrict_link_reject before using .ipe for policy verification. - Access the keyring directly instead of through a lookup helper, and panic if keyring allocation fails. - Explain the per-guest signing use case and the reason for avoiding a static private key in guest build artifacts. - Retain the well-known key ID commit, but refine its commit message. - Define the IPE acronym in kernel-parameters.txt. - Document the userspace-provisioned threat model and kexec requirements. - Drop the kselftest commit; instead, add tests to IPE CI's policy_signature batch [4]. - Link to v1: https://lore.kernel.org/r/user2@example.test
--- Manuel Huber (3): ipe: add the .ipe policy keyring keys: add KEY_SPEC_IPE_KEYRING Documentation: ipe: document the IPE keyring
Documentation/admin-guide/LSM/ipe.rst | 77 ++++++++++++++++++++++++- Documentation/admin-guide/kernel-parameters.txt | 1 + Documentation/security/ipe.rst | 19 ++++-- Documentation/security/keys/core.rst | 12 ++++ include/linux/key.h | 2 + include/uapi/linux/keyctl.h | 1 + security/ipe/Kconfig | 16 +++++ security/ipe/Makefile | 2 + security/ipe/ipe.c | 4 ++ security/ipe/keyring.c | 32 ++++++++++ security/ipe/keyring.h | 17 ++++++ security/ipe/policy.c | 17 ++++++ security/keys/process_keys.c | 23 ++++++++ 13 files changed, 217 insertions(+), 6 deletions(-) --- base-commit: 48f936e302a9c48cfc032eb5944c3a6246bc9043 change-id: 20261019-b4-ipe-keyring-rfc-b93b9ae129a2
Best regards, -- Manuel Huber <user5@example.test>

entry.title: [PATCH v2 1/3] ipe: add the .ipe policy keyring

div.pre:
From: Manuel Huber <user5@example.test>
Add a dedicated .ipe keyring for IPE policy signature verification. With this, userspace can provision its own keys into the keyring, then restrict it and activate it for IPE policy signature verification.
Gate creation of the keyring behind a new by-default disabled CONFIG_SECURITY_IPE_KEYRING Kconfig option. When created, the keyring is empty and writable. The keyring is used as a fallback after the existing policy trust sources only when it is created, non-empty, and restricted with restrict_link_reject.
This enables scenarios in which a trusted userspace component generates an IPE policy, and creates an ephemeral policy-signing key pair, provisions its public certificate, and restricts the IPE keyring during the early lifetime of a system. The trusted component can then sign the IPE policy, destroy the private key, and load and activate the policy. During that phase, the system is considered in a trusted state whereas the system transitions into a possibly untrusted state afterwards, running arbitrary user-provided applications. In such a scenario, the trusted userspace component could reside on a dm-verity protected rootfs disk, and applications would reside on additional dm-verity protected disks. The latter disks would be dynamically attached and their dm-verity root hashes and/or signatures not known a priori to launching the system.
A concrete usage scenario could be Kata Containers, which enables running Kubernetes pods in ephemeral, headless utility VMs, possibly without systemd. The rootfs disk is static and known beforehand, but containerd's image layers might be acquired and transported into the VM using the erofs snapshotter and dynamic block device attachment using dm-verity. While in that usage scenario, signing a per-guest policy with a pre-provisioned policy-signing certificate in the builtin, secondary, or platform keyrings would be technically possible, it would require including its corresponding private key in the guest build artifacts. Making it possible to use an ephemeral, userspace-provided key avoids shipping a static policy-signing private key with the guest rootfs.
Signed-off-by: Manuel Huber <user5@example.test> --- Documentation/admin-guide/kernel-parameters.txt | 1 + security/ipe/Kconfig | 16 +++++++++++++ security/ipe/Makefile | 2 ++ security/ipe/ipe.c | 4 ++++ security/ipe/keyring.c | 30 +++++++++++++++++++++++++ security/ipe/keyring.h | 17 ++++++++++++++ security/ipe/policy.c | 17 ++++++++++++++ 7 files changed, 87 insertions(+)
diff --git a/Documentation/admin-guide/kernel-parameters.txt b/Documentation/admin-guide/kernel-parameters.txt index e75344f4e0cd..9fabbc1c95b6 100644 --- a/Documentation/admin-guide/kernel-parameters.txt +++ b/Documentation/admin-guide/kernel-parameters.txt @@ -23,6 +23,7 @@ HW Appropriate hardware is enabled. HYPER_V HYPERV support is enabled. IMA Integrity measurement architecture is enabled. + IPE Integrity Policy Enforcement is enabled. IP_PNP IP DHCP, BOOTP, or RARP is enabled. IPV6 IPv6 support is enabled. ISAPNP ISA PnP code is enabled. diff --git a/security/ipe/Kconfig b/security/ipe/Kconfig index a110a6cd848b..5c51da074264 100644 --- a/security/ipe/Kconfig +++ b/security/ipe/Kconfig @@ -51,6 +51,22 @@ config IPE_POLICY_SIG_PLATFORM_KEYRING
If unsure, answer Y.
+config SECURITY_IPE_KEYRING + bool "IPE policy keyring" + default n + help + This option creates the .ipe keyring, which allows trusted + userspace to provision certificates for IPE policy signature + verification. IPE uses the keyring only after userspace has added + at least one certificate and applied a reject-all restriction. + + Enable this only when the userspace component that provisions and + restricts the keyring is part of the system's trusted computing + base. Such systems must also prevent unauthorized kexec, which + would start a new kernel without preserving the keyring state. + + If unsure, answer N. + menu "IPE Trust Providers"
config IPE_PROP_DM_VERITY diff --git a/security/ipe/Makefile b/security/ipe/Makefile index 2ffabfa63fe9..78161dfb48ea 100644 --- a/security/ipe/Makefile +++ b/security/ipe/Makefile @@ -25,6 +25,8 @@ obj-$(CONFIG_SECURITY_IPE) += \ policy_parser.o \ audit.o \
+obj-$(CONFIG_SECURITY_IPE_KEYRING) += keyring.o + clean-files := boot_policy.c \

All rights reserved. + */ + +#include <linux/cred.h> +#include <linux/err.h> +#include <linux/key.h> + +#include "keyring.h" + +struct key *ipe_keyring __ro_after_init; + +/** + * ipe_keyring_init() - Allocate and configure the IPE keyring. + * + * Return: Always %0. + */ +int __init ipe_keyring_init(void) +{ + ipe_keyring = + keyring_alloc(".ipe", GLOBAL_ROOT_UID, GLOBAL_ROOT_GID, + current_cred(), KEY_POS_SEARCH | + KEY_USR_VIEW | KEY_USR_READ | KEY_USR_WRITE | + KEY_USR_SEARCH | KEY_USR_SETATTR, + KEY_ALLOC_NOT_IN_QUOTA, NULL, NULL); + if (IS_ERR(ipe_keyring)) + panic("failed to allocate \".ipe\" keyring"); + return 0; +} diff --git a/security/ipe/keyring.h b/security/ipe/keyring.h new file mode 100644 index 000000000000..d9a057a14978 --- /dev/null +++ b/security/ipe/keyring.h @@ -0,0 +1,17 @@ +/* SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0 */ +/* + * Copyright (C) 2026 NVIDIA CORPORATION & AFFILIATES. new = kzalloc_obj(*new); @@ -188,6 +193,18 @@ struct ipe_policy *ipe_new_policy(const char *text, size_t textlen, VERIFY_USE_PLATFORM_KEYRING, VERIFYING_UNSPECIFIED_SIGNATURE, set_pkcs7_data, new); +#endif +#ifdef CONFIG_SECURITY_IPE_KEYRING + if (rc == -ENOKEY || rc == -EKEYREJECTED) { + restriction = READ_ONCE(ipe_keyring->restrict_link); + if (READ_ONCE(ipe_keyring->keys.nr_leaves_on_tree) && + restriction && + READ_ONCE(restriction->check) == restrict_link_reject) + rc = verify_pkcs7_signature(NULL, 0, new->pkcs7, + pkcs7len, ipe_keyring, + VERIFYING_UNSPECIFIED_SIGNATURE, + set_pkcs7_data, new); + } #endif if (rc) goto err;

entry.title: [PATCH v2 3/3] Documentation: ipe: document the IPE keyring

div.pre:
From: Manuel Huber <user5@example.test>
Document the .ipe policy-verification keyring with its additive use after the existing trust sources and the userspace's role in sustaining trust. Mention requirements for maintaining policy trust in kexec scenarios.
Signed-off-by: Manuel Huber <user5@example.test> --- Documentation/admin-guide/LSM/ipe.rst | 77 ++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++- Documentation/security/ipe.rst | 19 ++++++--- 2 files changed, 90 insertions(+), 6 deletions(-)
diff --git a/Documentation/admin-guide/LSM/ipe.rst b/Documentation/admin-guide/LSM/ipe.rst index 9e82a2082b94..273f9c3d62e2 100644 --- a/Documentation/admin-guide/LSM/ipe.rst +++ b/Documentation/admin-guide/LSM/ipe.rst @@ -150,6 +150,39 @@ Additionally, IPE draws hard security boundary between userspace and kernelspace. As a result, kernel-level exploits are considered outside the scope of IPE and mitigation is left to other mechanisms.
+Userspace-provisioned policy trust +~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ + +When ``CONFIG_SECURITY_IPE_KEYRING`` is enabled, IPE can authenticate policy +signatures with certificates provisioned into the ``.ipe`` keyring. This +differs from IPE's other policy trust sources, whose roots of trust originate +in the kernel image or firmware: the userspace component that provisions the +``.ipe`` keyring becomes part of the trusted computing base. + +That component must fulfill various requirements. The component must: + +- run before any untrusted userspace component runs +- be backed by code from a trusted location +- obtain its policy inputs from trusted sources +- complete provisioning without failures before allowing untrusted code to + run. This includes adding all intended certificates, applying the + reject-all keyring restriction, and removing the keyring permissions which + would allow later modification. +- destroy the policy-signing private key after signing the policy, if it + generated one. + +The ``.ipe`` keyring authenticates policy signatures; it does not make the +active policy immutable or otherwise change authorization for IPE's +securityfs control interfaces. + +Note on Kexec: Kexec bypasses firmware and bootloader trust checks and does +not preserve the ``.ipe`` keyring or active policy. Deployments must thus +prevent unauthorized kexec or establish equivalent trust in the replacement +environment, including any initramfs and command line. Controls that deny +further kexec loading do not prevent execution of an already-loaded image, +so any previously loaded image must satisfy the same trust requirements or +be unloaded before those controls take effect. + Policy ------
@@ -238,7 +271,12 @@ unconstrained root, and deploying an "allow all" policy). These policies must be signed by a certificate that chains to the ``SYSTEM_TRUSTED_KEYRING``, or to the secondary and/or platform keyrings if ``CONFIG_IPE_POLICY_SIG_SECONDARY_KEYRING`` and/or -``CONFIG_IPE_POLICY_SIG_PLATFORM_KEYRING`` are enabled, respectively. +``CONFIG_IPE_POLICY_SIG_PLATFORM_KEYRING`` are enabled, respectively. When +``CONFIG_SECURITY_IPE_KEYRING`` is enabled, IPE also provides a dedicated +``.ipe`` keyring for policy-signing certificates that are provisioned by +userspace, as described below. The ``.ipe`` keyring is an additive final +fallback and does not replace the configured system trust sources. + With openssl, the policy can be signed by::
openssl smime -sign \ @@ -251,6 +289,43 @@ With openssl, the policy can be signed by:: -outform der \ -out "$MY_POLICY.p7b"
+Provisioning the IPE policy keyring +^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ + +The ``.ipe`` keyring allows a system to provision an IPE-specific policy +signing certificate without embedding it in the kernel or firmware trust +stores. It is not linked into any process keyring. Userspace addresses it +directly with the ``KEY_SPEC_IPE_KEYRING`` special key ID (``-12``), which does +not grant possession of the keyring. + +The keyring exists when ``CONFIG_SECURITY_IPE_KEYRING`` is enabled and starts +empty and writable. If the option is disabled, using +``KEY_SPEC_IPE_KEYRING`` fails with ``ENOKEY``. Userspace can add a DER-encoded +X.509 certificate and then apply a reject-all restriction:: + + keyctl padd asymmetric "" -12 < policy-signing-key.der + keyctl restrict_keyring -12 + +Both steps are required. IPE ignores the keyring until it is nonempty and its +restriction is the reject-all restriction installed by the second command, so +a partially provisioned, mutable keyring is not a trust source. The +restriction cannot be removed. More than one certificate can be enrolled by +repeating the ``keyctl padd`` command before restricting the keyring. + +Restriction prevents adding keys, but it does not prevent userspace from +removing keys or otherwise disabling the keyring. To lock it against further +userspace modification, drop its write and setattr permissions:: + + keyctl setperm -12 0x08030000 + +This retains the permissions needed for verification and inspection. +Provisioning, restriction, and permission hardening must be completed as +described in `Userspace-provisioned policy trust`_ before relying on ``.ipe`` +as a trust source. + +Once nonempty and restricted, ``.ipe`` is searched after the configured system +trust sources. An absent, empty, or unrestricted ``.ipe`` keyring is ignored. + Deploying the policies is done through securityfs, through the ``new_policy`` node. To deploy a policy, simply cat the file into the securityfs node:: diff --git a/Documentation/security/ipe.rst b/Documentation/security/ipe.rst index 4490aed5918a..8afa8172c9ec 100644 --- a/Documentation/security/ipe.rst +++ b/Documentation/security/ipe.rst @@ -248,11 +248,20 @@ policy updates have to be done rebootlessly.
To allow an update from an external source, it could be potentially malicious, so this policy needs to have a way to be identified as trusted. This is -done via a signature chained to a trust source in the kernel. Arbitrarily, -this is the ``SYSTEM_TRUSTED_KEYRING``, a keyring that is initially -populated at kernel compile-time, as this matches the expectation that the -author of the compiled-in policy described above is the same entity that can -deploy policy updates. +done via a signature chained to a trust source in the kernel. IPE can use the +builtin trusted keyring and, when configured, the secondary and platform +keyrings. This matches systems where the entity that establishes the kernel or +firmware trust store is also authorized to deploy policy updates. + +When ``CONFIG_SECURITY_IPE_KEYRING`` is enabled, IPE also has a dedicated +``.ipe`` keyring for deployments that establish an IPE-specific trust anchor +from userspace. In this case, IPE uses it as a fallback after the configured +system keyrings, but only when it is nonempty and has a reject-all +restriction. This model makes the userspace component that provisions and +restricts ``.ipe`` part of the trusted computing base, for instance a +component running in early stages of the lifecycle of a system. The +threat model and provisioning requirements are documented in +:doc:`/admin-guide/LSM/ipe`.
Anti-Rollback / Anti-Replay ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
-- 2.53.0

div.pre:
On Thu, Oct 29, 2026 at 12:30:38AM +0000, Manuel Huber via B4 Relay wrote: > From: Manuel Huber <user5@example.test> > > Add a dedicated .ipe keyring for IPE policy signature verification. > With this, userspace can provision its own keys into the keyring, > then restrict it and activate it for IPE policy signature verification. > > Gate creation of the keyring behind a new by-default disabled > CONFIG_SECURITY_IPE_KEYRING Kconfig option. When created, the keyring > is empty and writable. The keyring is used as a fallback after the > existing policy trust sources only when it is created, non-empty, and > restricted with restrict_link_reject. > > This enables scenarios in which a trusted userspace component generates > an IPE policy, and creates an ephemeral policy-signing key pair, > provisions its public certificate, and restricts the IPE keyring during > the early lifetime of a system. The trusted component can then sign the > IPE policy, destroy the private key, and load and activate the policy. > During that phase, the system is considered in a trusted state whereas > the system transitions into a possibly untrusted state afterwards, > running arbitrary user-provided applications. In such a scenario, the > trusted userspace component could reside on a dm-verity protected > rootfs disk, and applications would reside on additional dm-verity > protected disks. The latter disks would be dynamically attached and > their dm-verity root hashes and/or signatures not known a priori to > launching the system.
Not trying to muddy the water here, but I stared / thought about this a while and wonder if I'm missing something below...
With this Kconfig approach, aren't we now saying "if you want to use IPE, and you want to ever use this feature, you need to make sure you seal that keyring or else someone can replace the IPE policy!"? That seems rather easy to foobar, and means to me at most kernels (i.e. distros) won't have this enabled which limits how easy this is to use. I know Fan wanted this behind some Kconfig to make it controlled by build time, but does it make sense to keep the command line option as well to really make this opt-in for users who have it enabled at build time? Otherwise you really are gonna have to craft a special kernel in my mind.
Likewise, but more nitpicky, I'm not sure the restrict_link_reject requirement buys much over the chain restriction. restrict_link_reject stops new keys being added, but pkcs7_validate_trust() walks certs embedded in the signature, so whoever holds the private key of any cert in .ipe can sign a new leaf, embed it, and have a policy accepted anyway I believe. Under both restrictions that basically means "holders of an enrolled private key and whoever they delegate to". If the concern is a restriction like key_or_keyring:<id> pointing at a writable keyring, that seems like a provisioner bug rather than a reason to rule out the chain restriction. Am I missing another reason for the stricter check? I do realize this is rather pedantic in argument and doesn't have a place in the use case described, but I'm wondering if a future use case will want such a thing.
Thanks, Andrew

Making it possible to use an ephemeral, > userspace-provided key avoids shipping a static policy-signing private > key with the guest rootfs. >
Reading through this scenario again, I have a question about the design.
I suspect the reason you need a signing key inside the guest rootfs is that you are running the snapshotter inside the VM. Have you considered generating the snapshots on the VM host, signing the policy there, and passing it into the guest?
The workflow would be:
1. The host generates an ephemeral signing key pair for the VM and injects the public certificate into the guest's platform keyring via firmware. 2. The host prepares the image snapshots, computes their dm-verity root hashes, and signs the resulting IPE policy which allows execution by dm-verity root hash with the ephemeral private key. 3. The host attaches the snapshot block devices and passes the signed policy into the guest, where the guest simply loads and activates it against .platform.
That way no private key ever needs to live in the guest, and it confines the TCB to the VM host. Would this approach work for your setup?
Fan

entry.title: Re: [PATCH v2 1/3] ipe: add the .ipe policy keyring

div.pre:
On Wed, Nov 04, 2026 at 12:14:57PM -0800, Fan Wu wrote: > That way no private key ever needs to live in the guest, and it > confines the TCB to the VM host. Would this approach work for > your setup?
My main angle is confidential Kata containers [1], a usage scenario in which (Kubernetes) workload containers run in trusted, confidential VMs on untrusted hosts. This scenario involves hardware TEEs, attestation, and fine-grained policing of host-side inputs. Without getting into too many details, having an untrusted host bake trust anchors into the guest on the fly would undermine the threat model. The proposed IPE keyring gives the trusted guest the ability to construct and sign the IPE policy independently. Also note, outside of the confidential scenario for Kata containers, various Kata containers flavors are very opinionated on the guest boot flow, so I cannot rely on UEFI being present. Having a self-contained mechanism independent of firmware certificate provisioning would therefore be highly preferrable.
[1] https://confidentialcontainers.org/docs/architecture/
